newsitem.title: CROATIA: Albright meets Serb victims, gets tough on Croatia.
newsitem.headline: Albright meets Serb victims, gets tough on Croatia.

text.p: U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright saw at first hand on Saturday the result of attacks on ethnic Serbs who recently tried to return to the homes they had in Croatia before the1991 Croatia-Serbia war.

Standing in front of a burned-out house in Prevrsac, a village about 75 km (45 miles) southeast of Zagreb, Albright used the occasion to underline a strong message she had given earlier to President Franjo Tudjman -- that America expects Croatia to do more to honour pledges it has made over the rights of refugees.

"I'm shocked by what I've seen here. I've spoken about the subject in a general way for a long time but when you see what's happened and talk to a family -- people who wanted to come here and live in their own houses and now live like prisoners or with relatives -- I find it disgusting," Albright told reporters.
After talking at length with a family that was attacked two weeks ago, Albright spoke to Foreign Minister Mate Granic and Reconstruction Minister Jure Radic.

"I think it is the responsibility of your government to live up to what you say you're doing, which is to make sure there is freedom of movement. I hope you will send out a message loud and clear that this is not acceptable."

Earlier, at a meeting which U.S. officials described as the toughest she has had with any leader since becoming secretary of state in January, Albright told Tudjman it was morally unacceptable to have an ethnically pure state in modern Europe.
"Croatia will not travel the road to Europe unless all its peoples, Croats or Serbs, make the journey," she said.

She warned Croatia that, if it failed to meet pledges on refugees and war crimes and did not exercise "moral" leadership in the region, the United States would continue to oppose aid and other benefits.

Tudjman insisted Zagreb supported the right of Serbs to return to their homes. "For all practical purposes, Croatia is not embarking on any policy of ethnic purity but rather recognises fully all human and ethnic rights of all communities living in this country, including Serbs," he said.

The outbreak of violence earlier this month focused attention on government plans to resettle tens of thousands of displaced people, many of whom are still bitter and do not want to live in ethnically mixed communities.
Bosnian Croat refugees who moved into empty Serb homes in Prevrsac said they did not see why they should be thrown out to allow Serbs to come home.

"If the Serbs are able to come here, we want to be able to go back to our own houses, but if we can't go there the Serbs can't come here either. We will fight if necessary. Don't we have human rights as well?" said Luka Vuckovic.
Zagreb says the violence was provoked by the spontaneous and unannounced arrival of Serbs in several villages, but the United States accused local government officials of being involved.
Albright told reporters she thought it would be "useful" if some arrests were made in the area, adding that there had to be action rather than just talk.
The U.S. public dressing-down of the Zagreb government comes just two weeks before Tudjman stands for re-election and it is the latest in a series of such reprimands from Washington.
Two weeks ago Albright met Granic in Washington and made it plain the United States expected higher standards from Croatia if it was to achieve its aim of moving closer to the West.

Albright told Tudjman that, if he failed to honour commitments he made when signing the 1995 Dayton peace accord that ended the Bosnian war, the United States would consider blocking International Monetary Fund loans and Croatia's integration into Western institutions.
A U.S. official said later Albright told Tudjman she would personally approve how the United States voted at the IMF.
Her spokesman told reporters the only commitment Tudjman made was to open a bridge at Brcko, over the Sava River from the Bosnian Serb republic to Croatia, to open a trade route.
